Area.evidence_source: [page/13/Text/4] In addition to the assistance Victor received from his teacher, he also indicated that he received significant support from other L/B/G friends. The support that L/B/G youth are able to give each other may have special importance due to a sense of shared experience. [page/13/Text/6] L/G/B friendships can further help to assist resiliency by providing a forum to enable L/B/G youth to collectively find solutions to their common problems. For example, by joining a L/B/G support group, Sam was helped to gain the knowledge he needed to address his problems and strengthen self-esteem: [page/13/Text/7] I went to "Ice Breakers" which was really good, which was a major step, sort of like reclaim self esteem, like up until that point I had never met an openly gay person, you know it was a pretty major thing at 16, um, and that was just really good meeting other young gay people, and we talked a lot, and I read a lot of books and got a lot of information that just wasn't given to me, and that was just the turning point. (Sam, 19, non-attempter) [page/13/Text/8] Not only may support groups serve to "normalise" L/B/G sexualities, but they may also provide youth with role models of other young men who have traversed the various tasks of coming-out to reach positive resolutions. [page/13/Text/9] Support networks may also offer respite from hostile home environments by providing L/B/G youth with somewhere to stay during diffi- [page/14/Text/2] cult periods. In some cases this may prevent a life on the streets and the danger of a negative spiral that may include drugs and prostitution (Kruks, 1991). Indeed, all participants in the current study reported that after time and space (which varied from 1 week to 5 months) away from other family members, the family and young people often become comfortable with the idea of living together again. [page/14/Text/3] Another role played by such support structures in the development of resiliency factors for L/B/G youth, lies in their ability to provide safe sex information (see Kegeles, Hays, & Coates, 1996). Various participants reported fears around HIV/AIDS infection, and Carl demonstrates that such fears and associated suicide risk could be reduced by sexually transmitted infections (STIs) education: [page/14/Text/4] I kind of had an HIV scare, not so long ago, I sort of thought I was HIV positive and if I was going to be HIV positive, I was, there was no question I just was going to do it . . . I was going to hurt myself, I just couldn't think of it any other way, because I just didn't want my family to see me like this, I didn't want them to see me like that. ...I just did not want to live if I had HIV, lack of education, I wasn't educated about the subject, I kind of thought about AIDS um ...I love my nieces and nephews and am I still going to be able to play with them, and stuff, if I can't play with my younger generation then I just don't want to be a part of their lives at all . . . but that was then, I know a lot more now . . . once I got the negative statement, and she [the doctor] like totally educated me, and I was like oh okay. (Carl, 19, attempter)
